prize_parts.citation: For developing methods to estimate demand and market power in differentiated-product industries, with endogenous prices and heterogeneous consumers.

statement.case_for: Berry (1994) and Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (1995) made it possible to estimate demand for differentiated products when prices are endogenous and consumers are heterogeneous. This turned empirical industrial organization into a quantitative field in which markups, welfare and merger counterfactuals can be computed from market data. The tools are now routine in antitrust and merger review, and they are used in trade, health, environmental and public economics, so the influence is well outside one subfield. The work is about thirty years old, has been extended and criticised extensively, and has held up in practice. Attribution to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes is more compact than for several other shortlisted candidates, and Pakes's separate work on dynamic industry models supports his place without changing the citation. After reading my colleagues' openings I am keeping this as my first choice. I do so on influence and durability, not because other members rank it highly, and I treat B036 and B040 as close alternatives.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is chiefly a methodological contribution, and some members will judge it by a stricter standard for discovery. Structural estimates also depend on functional-form and instrument assumptions, so the credibility of particular applications is debated. The seven-name credited set leaves out Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin, whose claims to earlier or complementary strands of empirical IO are real, and a three-name cap forces a cut that some will see as arbitrary. Support for the candidate in the openings is also narrower than for B040, B044 or B036: it is ranked by only seven members and appears in three top-three lists. I do not treat that as a verdict on merit, but it is a practical risk for a configuration that depends on broad committee agreement.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B040 first because Kiyotaki and Moore give a clean two-person attribution and a foundational macro-finance mechanism. She notes that empirical validation of the mechanism is more mixed than its theoretical influence, and that the 2022 prize may overlap. She ranks B024 second but asks whether it is a methods prize or a prize for substantive discovery, and whether Bresnahan and Reiss deserve credit.
responses.response: I agree that B040 has the cleanest attribution of any shortlisted candidate, and her caveats about empirical validation and the 2022 overlap are the reasons I ranked it seventh. I now see it as a closer alternative than my opening ranking implied, and I list it as one. On methods versus discovery, I think the BLP framework counts as a substantive advance. It made markups, consumer welfare and merger effects measurable, and that changed what the field and regulators could know. I agree that Bresnahan and Reiss's earlier empirical entry work is a separate strand. It strains the three-name limit but does not change the core BLP credit.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B040 first, emphasising clean attribution to Kiyotaki and Moore and nearly three decades of use. He ranks B024 sixth on the grounds that Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are more peripheral to the core method, and he asks how much weight methodological contributions should carry.
responses.response: I agree that the core of B024 is the BLP trio, and that Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin should not be forced into a three-name award. Making that explicit is why my citation covers only demand estimation with endogenous prices and heterogeneous consumers. I would not credit the broader structural-IO programme. I do not think a clean theoretical mechanism should rank above an empirical framework only because the mechanism is simpler to state. The criterion should be what the contribution changed in practice and how long it has lasted, and on both BLP has a record comparable to B040.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B036 first. He argues that heterogeneous-firm trade changed the understanding of selection, reallocation and the gains from trade, and that the field has had no dedicated prize since 2008. He also flags that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are outside the credited set. He ranks B024 last among his eight, citing the large credited group, difficult attribution and its partly methodological character.
responses.response: I share his regard for B036, ranked it second, and propose the same pair, Helpman and Melitz. I qualify one point. The absence of a trade prize since 2008 bears on field balance, not on scientific merit, and I would not count it in B036's favour. His concern about omitted co-originators applies to B036 as well as B024, since Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum also fall outside its credited names. I think B024's three-name core of Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes is easier to identify than the size of the credited set suggests. I therefore keep B024 first and B036 as the principal alternative.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B002 first. He sees population-scale administrative data as changing how mobility is measured and as showing that childhood place matters causally, with a two-person Chetty and Hendren core. He acknowledges that long-run durability is still being tested and that credit within the wider Opportunity Insights team is hard to draw.
responses.response: I ranked B002 third, and the maturity point he concedes is what keeps it there. Most key results date from 2014 onward, and the causal interpretation of area effects is still being tested, so the track record is shorter than for B024, B036 or B040. His case for a two-person core is also stronger than my own three-name proposal. Several colleagues, including Dreber, Fredriksson and Hassler, limit credit to Chetty and Hendren, and I would not press for Friedman if B002 advanced. I would still prefer to wait for more evidence on long-run effects.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would credit only the BLP demand-estimation strand or the broader structural-IO programme, which would change both the names and the citation.
How much weight a methodological contribution should carry relative to a conceptual mechanism such as B040 or a framework such as B036, and whether the committee wants that kind of prize this year.
How the committee treats the omission of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin under the three-name limit.
How sensitive structural demand estimates are to functional-form and instrument assumptions, which I cannot assess here beyond general knowledge and the openings.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to any credited candidate on the shortlist is apparent from my supplied profile. I disclose that my research is in industrial organization and international trade, close to B024 and B036, and I have tried to judge them on the common criteria. I have co-authored with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen (IJIO 2026). Neither is a credited candidate, and I do not adjudicate it. My spouse's public political role is noted only as a public fact, with no apparent bearing on these ballots.
